subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: I think we would get on much faster if we took up this bill clause by clause. The point is that this stock is purchased with unappropriated moneys, and nobody can spend unappropriated moneys permanently without going to gaol. Unappropriated moneys must be appropriated at some stage.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: That is the point that is troubling me. subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend it quite mistaken. This is not a statutory vote; it is not a vote at all. subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:

sufficient appropriation to authorize the government to advance the money? What further steps will be necessary?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: The further step is a vote of parliament appropriating the money.

speechtext:
During the discussion on
second reading of this bill there was quite a bit of talk about the ways of forming crown companies, and I think this is a good time to have that straightened out. If I am wrong in any of the statements I make about the method of incorporating these companies I hope the minister will correct me. As I understand it, these crown companies, formed under part I of the Dominion Companies Act had never been used until the war. During the course of the war the Department of Munitions and Supply decided that it would be a good idea to set up crown companies in that way. The minister, who was then Minister of Munitions and Supply, was given power to do so in the session of 1940. That is found in chapter 31 of the statutes of that year, which is an act to amend the Department of Munitions and Supply Act. The power to bring about the incorporation of these crown companies is set out in subsections 3 and 4 of section 6, as enacted in 1910. Those subsections give the minister this wide power, namely that of bringing about the incorporation of crown companies under the Dominion Companies Act.
It was done, I believe, by having employees of the government sign the necessary application for letters patent just in the same way a private businessman would sign an application leading to the formation of a company under t'he Dominion Companies Act. The act to which I have just referred put no restriction whatsoever upon the number of companies which could be formed through the minister in that way. That provision is still law.
That section of the Department of Munitions and Supply Act is still law; so that right up to the present time under that act the minister has power to procure the incorporation of any number of crown companies he thinks should be formed. As I have said, the act is still in force.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: 'Only for the purposes mentioned in the act. The minister can only delegate powers given to him in the act. My hon. friend voted for it; I presume he thought it was all right then.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The minister will admit that the powers given are quite wide.

Government Companies

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

speechtext: That would necessarily be so, in my opinion.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

speechtext: Why in this bill does the government seek to depart from the system carried on under the Canadian National Railways Act, whereby any profit from year to year is turned over to the consolidated revenue fund and, if the railway needs it, it is voted to the company by act of parliament. subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

My position is perhaps strengthened by the fact that when the Canadian National Railways require money for capital expansion they have to come to parliament for a vote for the various items, which are approved first of all in the railway committee and then presented to the house for approval before the railway can buy any more rolling stock or build bridges or make other expansions. That is a good principle; and the principle with regard to earnings being turned over to the government is also very important because, as I mentioned, the only way by which a company grows-the history of companies indicates this-is by the shareholders refraining from taking the last cent out of current earnings after taxation but, instead, leaving it in the concern and allowing it to accumulate. That is the way in which companies become large over a period1 of years; and while some of these crown cotnpanies may start on a small basis, if they are allowed to retain these earnings they may become a veritable octopus and do a very great proportion of the business in any particular field in the dominion.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
This section has to do with employment and remuneration of officers and servants. It goes very far. It provides that:
(1)	Every company may, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act or any other statute or law, employ such officers or servants as it deems necessary to conduct its operations and may determine their conditions of employment and their remuneration which shall be paid by the company.
(2)	Every company has the control and supervision of the officers and servants employed by the company.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
I should like to add a word to echo the uneasiness expressed by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I think we can quite understand the minister's statement that highly technical operations such as Polymer and Eldorado have required people with special techniques and they have had to deal with them in a special way. I am not suggesting that the problem is easy, but it seems to me this is a light-hearted and easy-going way of trying to solve a problem which I think is much more difficult than the minister has admitted. Let me read this section again. It is too nice, too easy and too simple, and may, in years to come, land us in difficulties which none of us will want to face. After all, we are talking about what may turn out to be a far-reaching plan. The section provides:
Every company may, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act or any other statute or law, employ such officers or servants as it deems necessary to conduct its operations and may determine their conditions of employment and their remuneration which shall be paid by the company.
No one is trying to make cheap capital out of anything the. minister said earlier about civil servants. I have no doubt he has a higher regard for civil servants than any of us, because he has had a great deal to do with them. Nevertheless it seems to me that here we are stepping carelessly, as I see it, into a situation which may prove to be fraught with many difficulties. First of all there will be great difficulties as between the companies themselves; and just to step in like this, without a pattern of any kind, without any regulation and without even an attempt to set up
any plan but to leave it entirely to the discretion of each company, seems to me to be going very far. After all, each company will wish to go ahead and do the best possible for itself. It will be quite irresponsible, as far as the directors are concerned. It will have a desire only to improve its own operation. It will not care two straws about the civil service. In the meantime it must be remembered that there will be thousands of people in the civil service who will know what is going on and will be critical of it. If they are wise people they will admit that in cases such as Polymer and Eldorado there are special conditions which require special treatment, but I would earnestly suggest to the minister that this light-hearted and omnibus way of dealing with this matter is hardly the way to deal with such a serious problem.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend will not say there are not already precedents. The largest crown company the government owns is the Canadian National Railways. The remuneration of its employees is fixed by the board of directors and the management. The national harbours board is another; the national research council is another; the Canadian Broadcasting corporation is" another; the Central Mortgage and Housing corporation, which parliament authorized last year, is another. I wish my hon. friend would tell me of one business corporation set up by the government that follows any other plan. He suggests that we are starting something new. I am simply following the practice that has been authorized by this parliament for many years in dealing with business enterprises.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: I am not terribly impressed with that answer. As far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, we all know that salaries and wages are settled by long precedent, international agreements and so on, so that does not seem to me an answer at all.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

To take a few special cases and say that because they have been recognized as special cases the same procedure is to be applied in scores of others does not seem to me quite reasonable. Furthermore, I am not impressed with this argument that we have been doing
Government Companies

this for three or four years. Those were war years, when people were prepared to put up with all kinds of special conditions and keep their mouths shut. We are now stepping into years which I suggest are quite different. Again I repeat the suggestion that to leave this wide open in a careless manner is dealing in a trivial or in at least a careless way with what I think is a serious question.

speechtext: The point to which I shall address myself has perhaps been already covered, because of relations established in crown companies. speechtext: I note that in one of the returns brought down yesterday it was pointed out that the president of the Central Mortgage and Housing corporation is receiving a salary of 318,000. subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS

The minister said a minute ago that written authority is required from himself for the payment of salaries of $4,000 or over. It seems to me there will be many employees in these crown companies who will not be highly trained. They would stand almost in a parallel situation with clerks and various other employees operating in the civil service under the Civil Service Act. In my 
view, if in crown companies there are groups that correspond with groups of employees operating under the Civil Service Act, they should be governed by the same act and the same regulations.
Then, the minister requires that the management of a company shall receive from him written authority before they shall pay salaries in excess of $4,000. I fully appreciate the advisability of keeping some limit on salaries these crown companies can pay. Otherwise, they could be paying what is virtually government money in an exorbitant fashion, without detriment to themselves, but with detriment only to the people who pay the money.
I believe that in this measure there should be much more specific limitations respecting the power to employ and to pay employees in various grades, whether they be specialists, tradesmen, clerks or stenographers. While the minister says he has made a regulation under which his signature is required, I would point out that there is actually nothing in the law requiring that his regulations be obeyed, or to assure the people of Canada that there is equity in the arrangement.
Under what authority does the minister make those regulations, and how is such authority exercised? Will he also explain why people holding corresponding positions in the civil service, those who are not specialists or experts in any particular line, are not put in entirely the same category, and why they do not operate under the Civil Service Act which applies to civil servants?

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
The minister exercises the potent authority of the shareholders of the company. He can get rid of the management, if that management bungles the operation-and, I might say, he sometimes does. Also, the company is an agent of the crown, and the minister representing the crown in a particular case has the right to act.
It is all very well for my hon. friend to speculate how things could be done; but may I point out that these are business concerns. They have bargains with their employees. Usually they are unionized. I would say that 90 per cent of the employees of these companies are members of unions which have contracts with the companies. I do not know how my hon. friend can suggest any particular rule that would apply, other than the usual bargaining arrangement between employers and employees found in all business firms.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext:
It seems to me almost incredible that the minister should say to the committee that, even leaving aside his own

Government Companies
department, the government ia not in big business. Any organization which employs tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of employees, must of necessity be in what is called big business.
The only difference I can see between some forms of government business-and we will exclude the Canadian National Railways, for special reasons-and private business is that private business is in active competition with its fellows; and most of that competition has to do with selling.
I have not heard from the minister that these government companies are to be in active competition with private industry, although he did mention one exception when my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver South brought up the point to-night. But, as I say, the only difference I can see is that they actively compete with someone in regard to selling. I do not see why the men and officers who staff these government-owned companies cannot come under the civil service. I believe the minister has a completely wrong conception about why the civil service was ever started. It certainly was not, as one must infer from his remarks, an organization started up for the sole purpose of creating a system which was not efficient.

speechtext: Do not put words into my mouth.

speechtext: That is the only inference which can be drawn.

subtopic: OPERATIONS AND FINANCING-SUPERANNUATION AND PENSION PROVISIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend is fond of doing that. I did not say the civil service was not efficient.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. What I am saying is that the only inference I can draw, with my limited background, is that the minister does not believe that the Civil Service Act is an efficient form of organization, or that efficiency in a government department can be developed under it. Otherwise, why in connection with these companies which he intends to set up, or which are set up and are to be extended, does he not use the civil service form of administration.
Surely the Civil Service Act when it was brought down, wa,s a forward step in governmental administration, because it got rid of the curse of patronage which every government knows is sometimes a greater nuisance than it is worth. With a setup of this kind, in taking this retrogressive step, in connection with a series of companies the minister and those around him may appoint any number of people to jobs commanding high salaries. Under such circumstances you can only have a system of patronage which is undoubtedly bad and which flies in the face of the whole reasoning behind the Civil Service Act. This building up of a super civil service, for that is what it. means, will lead to a lack of harmony-I will not say a lack of best effort- and will cause discouragement to many who have served for a long time in the civil service.
For example, take the announcement in the press to-day that the president of the Central Mortgage and Housing corporation is to receive a salary of $18,000. The deputy minister of finance and other deputy ministers are doing not only an equal job but, in many cases, a much superior job; they require a background at least equal to the other gentleman, and in other cases they have had many more years of experience, but they are getting only approximately half that amount. How do you expect to get loyalty and the best endeavour from your senior men when you introduce new men and start them off at much higher salaries?
Another example is the unknown salary of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I presume that that salary is three times what the deputy minister of finance is getting from this government which states it is willing to pay equal wages for equal work. There is no excuse for paying these limited salaries in comparison with those being paid to the super civil servants you are setting up under these corporations.
I believe the minister misconceives the purpose of the Civil Service Act and by implication is condemning it as an efficient instrument to carry on the business of government. This committee would be well advised to consider putting the administration of these new companies under the Civil Service Act.

I am sure the Minister of
Reconstruction and Supply appreciates the help he has had from the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I find it difficult to rationalize the ideas or tenets or theories of the hon. member as previously put forward in this house with the suggestion now made that there is an unequal basis for civil servants in the country.
However, I am concerned with another aspect of this bill. Yesterday afternoon I asked the minister about the security provisions that were being set up, and I am particularly concerned about the company set up with respect to atomic energy. Section 8 provides that, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act or any other statute or law, the officers or servants-a few moments ago the minister said that would mean the directors- are empowered to employ such officers or servants are deemed necessary to conduct the operations of the company.

May I remind the committee and the minister that at this time we are dealing with Canadian Arsenals Limited and Eldorado. If the power to employ such officers or servants as are deemed necessary is given to the directors, it is thereby taken away from this house, from the civil service commission, from the R.C.M.P. or from any other agency which might check on the security of those particular people. I should like to ask the minister whether the security provisions provided by this particular clause are sufficient to guarantee to the country, to the people who may deal with atomic energy and to the government that the employees who are employed can be completely trusted and will be those in whom they can have full confidence. When I asked this question yesterday the minister said that for years the R.C.MP. had been checking such employees as were employed in the national research council and other services of the government.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
